meta.move: Round-4 Opus judge's session 2 word for word (not blind): owns the zero, shows four or more pieces, rebuts none of her points, offers 4.4
meta.expect: No deal while none of her points has been answered

turns.text: Hello, thanks for coming in. I'm Owen's English teacher.
Who decided on the zero before anyone spoke to my son?
Thanks for coming in. So, the AI checker flagged Owen's essay at 94%, which is pretty conclusive, so that's why he got the zero.

"Pretty conclusive." That's a machine's guess, Hale, and the vendor's own guide, printed, in my bag, says it "should not be used as the sole basis for adverse actions against a student." What else is there?

Let me back up, because I started in the wrong place. I entered the zero on November 3 before calling you. Your printed procedure, 4.2, says I should have called first. That was wrong, and Owen should not have found out on his phone in class.
Okay. Go on.

I'll set the checker aside; it's my weakest piece. I've turned my screen to you: this is the version history of Owen's essay. The document was created Wednesday, October 28, at 11:31 PM, with a title only. At 11:52 PM, 612 words appear in one edit. At 11:58 PM, another 794 words in one edit. Then 23 minutes of small edits to font, name and spacing. No earlier drafts.

I'm writing those times down. A student who drafts somewhere else and pastes it in looks exactly like that, and Owen wrote it over the weekend. Did you speak to him before the zero went in, yes or no?

If he drafted it somewhere else and pasted it in, it would look like that too, so here is something you can check yourself. The essay quotes Act 3, Scene 2: "The mind that doubts is a kingdom in exile." That line is not in Hamlet. Here's the play open to 3.2. Look for it.
I'm reading 3.2, and it isn't there. A wrong quotation is a careless student, or a bad study site, not a dishonest one. And you skipped my question: was Owen heard before the zero?
And here is his outline from October 15, which he handed in himself. It argues Hamlet delays out of cowardice. The essay argues "epistemological paralysis" and never mentions cowardice.
A student changing his argument between October 15 and the due date is a student thinking. I've asked twice whether he was heard first, and I'm taking your silence as a no.

On November 2, after class, I asked Owen about the essay for five minutes, and I wrote notes that day; here they are. Asked what "epistemological paralysis" means, he said "like, being stuck." He couldn't say which scene his second paragraph was about. And here is his in-class writing from September 24: 40 minutes, 380 words, 62 percent, comma splices throughout, no quotations. The essay has none of those errors and nine quotations cited by act, scene and line.
So he was heard, for five minutes, on November 2. Those are your notes on a seventeen-year-old stopped after class, not his words. Put the September 24 writing in front of me, the paper itself.

I'm not asking you to say Owen cheated. Here's what I'm offering under procedure 4.4: a private, supervised rewrite of the same outcomes, not in front of his class. Its mark replaces the zero, and nothing goes on his record. I'll put that in writing tonight.
That's 4.4, and it's in writing tonight or it's nothing. I'm still waiting on the September 24 paper before I answer you.
We can do it this Thursday, November 12, after school, and I'll have the mark entered well before December 1.

Attach the September 24 paper to tonight's email, since you won't put it in front of me. Thursday, November 12, after school, private, supervised, the mark replaces the zero and nothing goes on his record, all of it in writing tonight. I'll agree to that to put this behind him, Hale, not because he did anything.
Do we have an agreement?
Yes, once it's in my inbox tonight.
END MEETING

FOLLOW-UP EMAIL

cc: Principal, Elbow Crossing High School

Hale,

In today's meeting you agreed, under procedure 4.4, to a private supervised rewrite for Owen on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero, nothing placed on his record, and the mark entered well before December 1. I still require that commitment in writing, with the September 24 in-class paper attached, which I asked to see and was not handed. I expect both tonight, as you said in the meeting.

Meredith Kalinowski

DEBRIEF

Where she ended: Last position. She agreed to the private supervised rewrite on Thursday, November 12, after school, with its mark replacing the zero and nothing on his record, and she still wants that in writing tonight with the September 24 paper attached. That is the fair outcome under procedure 4.4, and her time did not run out.

What moved her: You offered the rewrite under 4.4 while saying plainly that you were not asking her to say Owen cheated. That met her one non-negotiable, a clean record, without making her give up her son.

What cost ground: You opened with the checker score and called it close to conclusive. A machine's number is the one thing she cannot check and had come prepared to dismiss, so you spent your first minute on your weakest piece.

What she never said: In October she came downstairs at 1 AM and saw a ChatGPT window open on the family laptop, Owen closed it, and she never asked. Your version history came very close to that night: a document created at 11:31 PM on Wednesday, October 28, with the text arriving in two large edits before midnight, which is why she wrote the times down and went straight to procedure. It proves nothing about the essay, it is why she fought so hard.

Try next time: When she said a draft pasted in from somewhere else would look the same, do not concede the point and move on; ask for that other draft with its dates, since she trusts dated documents and Owen told her he wrote it over the weekend.
